question: Before Coca-Cola became a bottled drink sold worldwide, where was it first served?
note: Pharmacist John Pemberton took his syrup to Jacobs’ Pharmacy in Atlanta in 1886. Mixed with carbonated water, it sold for five cents a glass; the company’s history records about nine drinks a day in the first year.

question: Chocolate-chip cookies existed before bags of chocolate chips. What went into the early recipe?
choices: A chocolate bar chopped into pieces
Cocoa powder rolled into little balls
note: Ruth Wakefield’s recipe told bakers to chop a chocolate bar into pea-sized pieces. Its popularity helped create a market for ready-made chocolate morsels: the cookie came before its now-familiar ingredient.

question: The fortune cookie looks like a Chinese tradition. In which country did it become a familiar restaurant dessert?
note: Its early history includes Japanese American and Chinese American businesses in California, with competing claims to its invention. By the 1930s, Chinese restaurants in America were giving the cookies away after meals; the familiar pairing grew there.

question: Some early cinemas kept popcorn out. What helped turn it into the classic movie snack during the Great Depression?
choices: It was cheap for audiences and profitable to sell
Film studios bundled it with their ticket deals
Cinema owners received it through food-relief programmes
Doctors promoted it as healthier than other sweets
note: Some cinemas had wanted to protect their carpets and their grand-theatre atmosphere. During the Depression, inexpensive popcorn brought in income that ticket sales alone could not; a snack once sold outside helped keep theatres open.

question: A hamburger is usually made with beef. Where does the “ham” in its name come from?
choices: A cut of pork in the earliest recipe
The surname of an American cook
An old English word for minced meat
note: Hamburger means “of Hamburg” in German. Hamburg-style beef dishes preceded the American sandwich, whose exact inventor remains disputed; the name does not require any ham.

question: Before McDonald’s golden arches became a logo, where would customers have seen them?
choices: Printed on the first hamburger wrappers
note: The early restaurant design had huge arches that drivers could spot from the road. Those architectural features became the symbol on the packaging: the building helped create the logo.

question: The microwave oven grew out of an engineer’s work on which technology?
note: While working with radar, Percy Spencer noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had melted. Experiments with food led to an oven: equipment designed to detect distant objects helped produce a new way to heat dinner.

question: Caesar salad sounds Roman and appears on American menus. Where was it created?
note: The generally accepted account places it at Caesar Cardini’s restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico. The Italian immigrant served Americans crossing the border during Prohibition; the familiar story joins three countries, and the name refers to Cardini, not Julius Caesar.

question: How did SPAM, an American canned meat, help give unwanted online messages their name?
choices: A comedy sketch repeated its name relentlessly
Its maker sent the first mass advertising email
Early computers used its name for spoiled data
A coupon campaign filled people’s mailboxes
note: In a Monty Python sketch, chanting of “Spam” overwhelms the conversation. Internet users borrowed the name for messages that similarly crowd out what people actually want to read.

question: During World War II, M&M’s were sold exclusively to which group?
note: Their candy shells helped make chocolate practical to carry in soldiers’ rations. The sweets later reached the civilian market, so a familiar cinema-counter treat had an earlier life in military supplies.

question: What lies at the Statue of Liberty’s feet, mostly hidden from visitors below?
note: The broken chains refer to the abolition of slavery, a detail easily missed in photographs taken from below. Her raised right heel also shows her stepping forward; this familiar statue is not simply standing still.

question: Before San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge became famous for its orange colour, what did the US Navy want it to look like?
note: The Navy wanted the bridge to be easy to see. The architect argued for orange-red instead, a colour that would stand out while fitting the surrounding hills and water.

question: New York welcomes the new year by lowering a glowing ball in Times Square. Earlier “time balls” helped people do what?
choices: Signal the start of horse races
Announce the closing of stock markets
note: A ball dropped at a known time gave ships a visible signal for setting their clocks. Times Square turned that practical time signal into a celebration, using its first illuminated ball after the city stopped its New Year fireworks.

question: The Hollywood Sign is now a symbol of cinema. What did it originally advertise?
choices: A railway to the film studios
note: The sign went up in 1923 as HOLLYWOODLAND, promoting a real-estate development. The surviving name acquired a much wider meaning than the property advertisement.

question: The film Cars shows a roadside town that travellers have forgotten. What happened to many real towns along Route 66?
choices: New highways carried traffic around them
Airports bought up their roadside businesses
National parks closed their roads to cars
Rail companies bought the road and removed it
note: Pixar researched Route 66 when creating its fictional town. Faster interstate highways bypassed many places whose diners, motels and shops had depended on passing drivers; the film’s deserted main street has a real history.

question: Chicago engineers made their river run backwards. What were they trying to protect?
note: The river carried sewage into Lake Michigan, which also supplied the city’s drinking water. A canal redirected the flow towards other rivers; Chicago solved a local problem by sending its pollution downstream.

question: Three men escaping from Alcatraz in 1962 needed guards to think they were still asleep. What did they leave on their pillows?
choices: Inflated rubber masks from a workshop
note: They made convincing heads using materials including soap, cotton and real hair. The men escaped their cells and disappeared; whether they survived the water crossing remains unresolved.

question: What unusual arrival did the Empire State Building’s designers once propose for its upper tower?
choices: Cable cars arriving from another skyscraper
Aeroplanes docking with a rooftop rail
note: The proposed mast would let airships moor above Manhattan and passengers descend by lift. The wind made the idea impractical, but the extra height helped the building overtake its skyscraper rival.

question: The Grand Canyon looks dry, yet its rocks contain seashell fossils. What explains them?
choices: Glaciers transported shells from the coast
Early settlers brought shells as building material
note: Many of the canyon’s rock layers formed in ancient marine environments, long before the river cut through them. Some shells are visible near the rim: a desert viewpoint can also be a window into an old seabed.

question: Las Vegas means “the meadows” in Spanish. Why does a desert city have that name?
choices: Natural springs once fed grassy areas
Early casinos planted lawns to attract visitors
It was named after a meadow in Spain
A railway company invented a greener-sounding name
note: Springs created an oasis used by Southern Paiute people long before the casinos. Traders later stopped for water and grass; the city’s name preserves a landscape that neon-lit photographs rarely show.

question: Before colonists threw British tea into Boston Harbour, a new law had changed its price. Which surprising change had it made?
choices: Set the same price as coffee
note: The Tea Act let the East India Company sell more cheaply, even with the tax. The protest concerned Parliament’s right to tax the colonies and the company’s privileged position; an affordable price did not settle the argument.

question: The Fourth of July celebrates American independence. What happened on that day in 1776?
choices: Congress adopted a declaration of independence
The last British troops left America
note: The date marks a declaration, not the end of the fight. Britain recognised American independence in the 1783 Treaty of Paris, years after the occasion now celebrated with fireworks.

question: The cowboy seems unmistakably American. Which earlier tradition helped supply the riding skills and equipment of the American West?
note: Mexican vaqueros worked cattle long before the familiar American cowboy era. Their techniques and equipment spread through the Southwest; the image seen in Western films owes much to this cross-border history.

question: Which present-day state did the United States buy from Russia for $7.2 million?
note: The United States agreed to buy Alaska in 1867 for $7.2 million. The National Archives still holds the payment cheque: a vast piece of the modern American map changed hands through a purchase.

question: The teddy bear took its name from President Theodore Roosevelt. What event helped turn his nickname into a toy?
choices: He refused to shoot a bear tied up for him
He kept a rescued bear at the White House
He gave toy bears to visiting children
He used a bear as his election symbol
note: A cartoon about the hunting incident inspired American shopkeepers to sell “Teddy’s bear”. The cartoon softened a grim event: Roosevelt declined to claim the injured animal as a hunting trophy, but it was subsequently killed.

question: George Washington’s false teeth were famously uncomfortable. What did the surviving sets actually contain?
note: They included animal and human teeth, rather than the wooden dentures of popular legend. The people whose teeth were used are not known; the objects also reveal an uncomfortable part of eighteenth-century dentistry.

question: A familiar immigration story says US officials shortened foreign surnames at Ellis Island. What do the records suggest?
choices: Names were generally checked against existing passenger lists
Long surnames were routinely shortened at the desk
Names were translated into English before inspection
Families drew new surnames from an approved list
note: Ship passenger lists had been prepared before arrival, and inspectors checked people against them. Families often changed their names later; the memorable story of an official inventing an American surname usually puts the change in the wrong place.

question: Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech became famous worldwide. What is surprising about its best-known section?
choices: He moved away from his prepared text
A newspaper added those lines afterwards
The audience sang it while he listened
It was recorded later because the microphone failed
note: King had used the dream theme in earlier speeches, but it was not in the prepared version he brought to the March on Washington. In front of the crowd he returned to that material and did not go back to the manuscript.

question: People escaping slavery in America travelled on the “Underground Railroad”. What was it?
choices: A network of routes and safe houses
A secret service using freight trains
A chain of tunnels beneath border towns
A fleet of boats with a railway cover name
note: It was a secret network of people, routes and places of refuge, rather than a railway. Harriet Tubman escaped slavery herself and repeatedly returned to guide others to freedom.

question: In Apollo photographs, the American flag spreads out on the airless Moon. What holds it out?
choices: A horizontal rod along its upper edge
Stiff material woven into the whole flag
A second pole hidden behind its far edge
A jet of air released by the astronauts
note: The flag needed a crossbar because there was no wind to lift it. On Apollo 11 the rod did not extend fully, leaving wrinkles that made the still flag look as though it was fluttering.

question: Some Soviet fans could not legally buy the American jazz and rock music they wanted. What did bootleggers reuse to make playable records?
note: They cut grooves into used X-ray film, so a record could show someone’s ribs or skull. These fragile discs circulated forbidden music; tape recorders later displaced the craft.

question: Early hip-hop DJs used two copies of a record to keep dancers moving. Which part did they stretch out?
choices: The drum-led passage between the vocals
The quiet opening before the beat
The final sustained note of the song
note: By switching between records, DJs could repeat a short instrumental break instead of letting it end. A few seconds inside an existing song became a longer space for dancers, helping shape hip-hop.

question: Why do we call a collection of recorded songs an “album”, the same word used for a book of photographs?
choices: Records were collected in books of sleeves
Early recordings came free with photo albums
Listeners pasted song lyrics into scrapbooks
Singers sold portraits instead of cover artwork
note: Early discs held only a few minutes per side, so a longer work could require several records in a bound album. Columbia’s long-playing record arrived in 1948, but the old name survived the change of format.

question: Dr. Seuss, the Grinch’s creator, wrote Green Eggs and Ham to win a bet. What restriction did he accept?
choices: Finish it in a single weekend
Write it without the letter E
note: His publisher offered a $50 wager: could Seuss write a book using only 50 different words? He built the whole story from that small vocabulary; the limitation helped create a book children could read for themselves.

question: Before people sang “Happy Birthday to You” over a cake, its melody belonged to what kind of song?
choices: A lullaby for putting babies to sleep
A song for welcoming wedding guests
A hymn sung at the end of a service
note: Mildred and Patty Hill published “Good Morning to All” for young children in Kentucky. Birthday words later took over the tune; who first made that change is uncertain.

question: Mark Twain, the author of Tom Sawyer, had worked on riverboats. What did the phrase he chose as his pen name measure?
choices: The weight of a boat’s cargo
note: “Mark twain” was a river call meaning two fathoms, about twelve feet of water. Samuel Clemens carried a piece of his old job into the name printed on his books.

question: The Great Gatsby sold modestly before it became a classic. What helped it reach a new audience during World War II?
choices: Pocket editions sent to service members
A film adaptation shown in military camps
Radio readings broadcast to troops overseas
Newspaper instalments printed for wartime readers
note: Pocket-sized Armed Services Editions put the novel into soldiers’ hands after Fitzgerald’s death. The book’s path to becoming a classic included wartime readers who had been given it for free.

question: Starbucks took its name from a character in which sea adventure?
note: Starbuck is the first mate in Moby-Dick. The founders also considered the ship’s name, Pequod; they wanted a link to adventure and the seafaring world of early coffee traders.

question: Andy Warhol painted 32 nearly identical soup cans. Why did he choose that number?
choices: There was one for each flavour the company sold
He painted one for each year of his life
He used one for each shop that sponsored the show
There was one for each country selling the brand
note: Each canvas shows a different Campbell’s soup variety available at the time. The paintings were first displayed on shelves like groceries, bringing the supermarket into an art gallery.

question: The United States’ national anthem uses a melody that began as what?
note: Before it accompanied American patriotic words, the tune belonged to a London music club. A British melody became the US anthem through words about an American fort surviving a British attack.

question: The first basketball game used a soccer ball. What did the players aim at?
note: James Naismith needed an indoor winter game, and a janitor found him two peach baskets. Their bottoms were still in place, so someone had to retrieve the ball after a goal; cutting out the bottoms came later.

question: A Nike co-founder experimented with a kitchen tool to make a new running-shoe sole. What did he use?
note: Bill Bowerman tried moulding a running-shoe sole in a waffle iron. His first attempt glued it shut, but later experiments produced a grid-patterned sole used on Nike’s early Moon Shoe.

question: During World War II, what replaced metal in Oscar statuettes because of shortages?
note: For three years the winners received plaster figures. After the war, the Academy invited recipients to exchange them for gold-plated metal statuettes.

question: Darth Vader’s mechanical breathing in Star Wars came from a recording made with what?
choices: An accordion slowly opening and closing
note: Sound designer Ben Burtt put a microphone inside a diving regulator and recorded himself breathing through it. One of cinema’s most recognisable villains gets part of his sound from equipment made for breathing underwater.

question: The small metal studs at the corners of jeans pockets began as a solution to what problem?
choices: Work trousers tearing at the seams
Loose coins wearing holes in the cloth
note: Jacob Davis used rivets to reinforce places that tore under hard use, then patented the method with Levi Strauss in 1873. A practical feature of workers’ clothing became a detail on jeans worn around the world.

question: Dorothy’s shoes are ruby red in The Wizard of Oz film. What colour were they in the book?
note: The film changed the silver shoes to ruby red for Technicolor. The red slippers against the yellow brick road became so familiar that the original version now feels like the surprising one.

question: The Simpsons live in Springfield, but the show keeps its location elusive. Why was that name useful?
choices: Many viewers could imagine it was their town
It was where the original animation studio stood
It was the hometown of the first voice actor
It was the location of his favourite comic-book shop
note: Springfield is a common American place name, so viewers in different places could imagine the cartoon town was theirs. As a child, creator Matt Groening had made a similar assumption about the Springfield in another television series.

question: Monopoly rewards players who collect rent and bankrupt their rivals. What was its ancestor, The Landlord’s Game, meant to demonstrate?
choices: How property monopolies make others poorer
How to negotiate a better mortgage
How a town should divide its building plots
How a family can save for its first home
note: Inventor Lizzie Magie used the game to show how landlords could prosper at tenants’ expense. Monopoly’s later success as a race to own everything often obscured that original warning.

question: Before streaming, how did a Netflix film reach your home?
choices: As a DVD delivered by post
As a download sent through email
As a VHS tape delivered by a local shop
As a scheduled broadcast on a cable channel
note: Customers chose films online, then waited for discs to arrive in red envelopes. When Netflix announced the end of its DVD service in 2023, it had lasted 25 years, overlapping with the streaming era.

question: Before the glowing Halloween pumpkin, people in Ireland carved faces into which vegetable?
note: Irish lanterns were often carved from turnips. Related customs travelled to North America, where the larger pumpkin was easier to hollow out; an older tradition acquired the face now familiar from American films.
